newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia shows off armed forces in holiday parade.
newsitem.headline: Croatia shows off armed forces in holiday parade.

text.p: Croatia staged a huge military parade to celebrate its Statehood Day national holiday on Friday, intended to show the country has a modern army ready for the 21st century and up to NATO standards.
President Franjo Tudjman, wearing the brown uniform of the supreme commander of the Croatian army, kick-started the one-hour multi-media event by pressing a computer button.
While tanks, rockets and towed guns processed past a VIP stand at Zagreb's main sports centre, television screens carried live aerial pictures of ships in the Adriatic Sea.

The highlight of the event was a manoeuvre by commando teams who were dropped from helicopters and dived off speedboats, then took control of an island against a background of mock explosions and smoke bombs.

The display was meant to prove the army, which routed Serb armies in Croatia and Bosnia in a series of surprise offensives in 1995, is now capable of waging integral air-land battles up to NATO standards.
Croatian victories in 1995 softened Serbian intransigence and set the stage for the U.S.-brokered Dayton peace agreement which ended 4-1/2 years of war in former Yugoslavia.
After agreeing that the last Serb-held enclave of Eastern Slavonia will come under Zagreb rule peacefully, Croatia is unlikely to engage in another military operation on its soil in the near future.
Its prime interest now is membership of the European Union and NATO, and top Croatian military officials claim the army has satisfied technical conditions for full membership of the alliance.
The parade was also a good opportunity for 75-year-old Tudjman, who faces re-election on June 15, to spend an hour on the television screens of potential voters.
Tudjman is tipped to win easily with more than 50 percent of the vote, which would give him a third term in office.
On this day six years ago, the first democratically-elected Croatian parliament held its opening session while Croatia was still a republic of former communist Yugoslavia.
